paras: The Limestone bank robbery lynching was the reported hanging of an unnamed robber by a "Judge Lynch" court at Limestone, Indian Territory, in January 1888, after four masked men robbed the Citizens' Bank and killed its cashier, W. T. Reynolds. According to a widely reprinted despatch, a second robber, Thomas Evan, was shot dead in a gunfight with townspeople, and the two remaining robbers were sent to Fort Washita for the federal authorities. The story ran in papers from South Carolina to Wyoming, but a letter from Atoka printed in the Fort Worth Gazette said there had never been a bank, or a town, at Limestone Gap.

Every account traces to one despatch datelined Limestone, January 23, which the New York Sun credited to the Chicago Times. A fuller version, printed as "a special despatch" in the Daily Republican, described the robbers as "citizens and cattle ranchers of the near neighborhood" and said crime had been traced to their doors before. It added that one of Evan's brothers had been hanged by vigilantes for cattle stealing the previous spring and another was in jail at Fort Smith, Arkansas.

According to the despatch, four armed, masked men entered the Citizens' Bank on Saturday, January 21, and demanded the cash at pistol point. Reynolds instead slammed and locked the safe and was shot above the heart and killed. The robbers took about $2,300 from the cash drawer but failed to open the safe.

Townspeople fired on by robbers standing guard went for arms, and twenty or thirty armed men came back; in the exchange of fire as the robbers mounted, Thomas Evan, identified as "a ranchman living near town," was killed and four citizens were wounded, none fatally. The three survivors fled toward Atoka with the money.

A posse caught them after about an hour's chase and took them back to Limestone, where, in the despatch's words, "Judge Lynch was called on to hold court." The leader, named in no account, was found guilty of Reynolds's murder and "forthwith strung up"; the True Northerner said he was hanged to a tree. The other two were sent under guard to Fort Washita to be turned over to the United States authorities, and the stolen money was recovered.
No report of an inquest, of any arrest of the men who hanged the leader, or of the two prisoners reaching Fort Washita appears in the coverage.

The Memphis Appeal ran it on January 24 under "Died at His Post," and the Emporia Weekly News, the Red Cloud Chief and the Barton County Democrat stacked headlines announcing a cashier killed and the leader lynched. By February 1 the Laurens Advertiser and the Manning Times in South Carolina had retitled it "Hero and Martyr," with the subhead "A Bank Cashier Killed by Robbers and Avenged by Lynchers," and the Fairfield News and Herald ran the same text. Papers in Ohio, Oregon and Rhode Island also reprinted it.

The Tombstone Epitaph placed the robbery at "Lone Stone" and put the sum taken at $20,000, while the Sully County Watchman in Dakota said the raid came on "Saturday night" and that the cashier and one robber were shot dead. The Sheridan Enterprise in Wyoming reported that pursuit resulted in "two robbers being killed" as well as the lynching of Reynolds's killer. No version mentioned anyone's race or commented on the hanging beyond its headlines.

The only challenge came in the Fort Worth Gazette. On February 4 it printed a letter from Atoka signed R. W. Officer under the heading "No Truth In It," followed by the original despatch under the heading "Faithful and False."

The Atoka letter said there was not, and had never been, a bank at Limestone Gap or anywhere else in the Indian Territory. Its writer described Limestone Gap as only a mountain cut by the Missouri, Kansas and Texas Railroad, with no town, and called the story a false statement. No reply, retraction or local confirmation of either side appears in the coverage.
The accounts also differ in detail: the robber's surname appears as Evan, Evans and Ewen, and the Daily Republican's text timed the raid at "about eleven o'clock yesterday" rather than Saturday.

reader.title: Limestone bank robbery lynching
bases: The despatch reports a posse captured fleeing robbers and hanged their leader after a 'Judge Lynch' court found him guilty of the cashier's murder (A1, A3); the event's reality is disputed (A18).

As reported, a posse drawn from twenty or thirty armed townsmen held a 'Judge Lynch' court and hanged the leader for the cashier's murder, meeting every element (A1, A3); but an Atoka letter says no bank or town existed at Limestone Gap (A18), and every account derives from one despatch, so the killing itself is unconfirmed.
All reports (A1, A3, A12, A13 and the briefs) reprint or rewrite one January 23 despatch, and a letter from Atoka denies that any bank or town existed at Limestone Gap (A18).

accounts.gist: Same story, timed 'about eleven o'clock yesterday', with the three tried that night and the robbers described as neighborhood cattle ranchers with a family record of crime.

accounts.label: Atoka letter (R. W. Officer)
accounts.gist: No bank has ever existed at Limestone Gap or in the Indian Territory; it is a railroad cut with no town, and the story is false.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the despatch verbatim under heads such as 'Died at His Post', 'Bank Robbers' and 'One Robber Shot, Another Hanged and Two Jailed', with no comment on the hanging.
South Carolina weeklies titled it 'Hero and Martyr' with the subhead 'A Bank Cashier Killed by Robbers and Avenged by Lynchers', casting the cashier as hero and the lynchers as avengers.
The Fort Worth Gazette reprinted the story as 'Faithful and False' directly after a reader's letter headed 'No Truth In It' denying it.
